title: Arrays
summary: An **array** in Go is a fixed-size, contiguous block of elements whose **length is part of its type** — `[3]int` and `[4]int` are different types. Arrays are **value types**: assigning or passing one copies every element. You rarely use arrays directly (slices are preferred), but they are the backing store behind slices and the right tool for fixed-size data like `[32]byte` hashes.
nestedConcepts: length is part of the type

subtopics.title: Length is part of the type
subtopics.explanation: An array's type includes its length: [3]int and [4]int are distinct, incompatible types. The length must be a compile-time constant, so the size is fixed and known when the program is built — you cannot grow or shrink an array. This rigidity is the defining trait of every Go array.

subtopics.title: Arrays are value types (they copy)
subtopics.explanation: Assigning one array to another, or passing an array to a function, copies ALL of its elements. The copy is independent — mutating it does not affect the original. This is the key contrast with slices, which share a backing array, and it is the single most important behavior to internalize about arrays.

subtopics.title: Zero values on declaration
subtopics.explanation: Declaring an array without an initializer fills every element with the element type's zero value: 0 for numbers, "" for strings, false for bools. There is no 'uninitialized' garbage in Go. This means an array is always usable the moment it is declared.

subtopics.title: Array literals and the ... ellipsis
subtopics.explanation: Write [3]int{1, 2, 3} to create and fill an array. Use [...]int{1, 2, 3} to let the compiler count the elements and set the length for you — the result is still a fixed-size array, not a slice. These literals are the idiomatic way to build an array with initial values.

subtopics.title: Indexing, bounds & comparison
subtopics.explanation: Index with a[i] starting at 0. A constant index outside the array is a compile error; a variable index out of range panics at runtime. Arrays of comparable element types can be compared with == (element-by-element). Both traits flow directly from an array being a fixed-size value.

subtopics.title: Arrays behind slices
subtopics.explanation: Every slice is a view over a backing array. Fixed-size arrays also shine for crypto hashes ([32]byte), UUIDs ([16]byte), and lookup tables where the size is genuinely constant. Understanding arrays therefore underpins how slices — Go's everyday sequence type — actually work.

foundations.overview: An array is the simplest aggregate type in Go: a fixed number of elements of the same type, laid out one after another in a single contiguous block of memory. The number of elements — the length — is baked into the type itself, so [3]int is a genuinely different type from [4]int. Because an array is a value, copying it copies every element. Most day-to-day Go code reaches for slices instead, but understanding arrays is essential because a slice is just a flexible window onto an underlying array.
foundations.formalDefinition: An array is a numbered, fixed-length sequence of elements of a single type, where the length is a constant that forms part of the array's type.
foundations.whyItMatters: Arrays teach the value-copy semantics and fixed-size memory layout that the rest of Go builds on. They power slices, and they remain the correct choice for fixed-width data such as hashes and UUIDs. The array-vs-slice distinction is one of the most common Go interview questions.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture an egg carton with a fixed number of slots, all created empty (zero values). The carton's size is stamped on it forever — a six-egg carton can never become a twelve-egg one. Hand the whole carton to someone and they get a complete duplicate, eggs and all; scribbling on their copy never touches yours.
commonUseCases: Small constant lookup tables indexed by enum or byte
The backing array that a slice views
Stack-allocated scratch buffers of known size

commonMisconceptions.myth: [3]int and [4]int are the same type with different sizes.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They are completely distinct types. A function taking [3]int cannot accept a [4]int, which is why fixed-length arrays are inflexible and slices are usually preferred.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Passing an array to a function lets the function modify the original.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The function receives a full copy; mutations don't escape. Pass *[N]T or a slice if you need the caller to see changes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Arrays and slices are basically interchangeable.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Arrays are fixed-size value types that copy; slices are growable reference-like views that share a backing array. The semantics differ in ways that cause real bugs.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Out-of-range access is always a compile error.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only constant indices are caught at compile time; a variable index out of range panics at runtime with 'index out of range'.

visualExplorer.title: How an array lives in memory (and what copying does)
visualExplorer.caption: An array is a contiguous block whose length is part of its type; assigning it duplicates every element.

config.intro: Follow a [3]int from declaration through a value copy:

steps.name: Declare
steps.detail: `var a [3]int` reserves three contiguous int slots and zeroes them: [0 0 0]. The length 3 is fixed and part of a's type.

steps.name: Fill
steps.detail: `a = [3]int{10, 20, 30}` writes the three elements in place — still the same contiguous block, no allocation or indirection.

steps.name: Copy on assign
steps.detail: `b := a` allocates a second three-slot block and copies all three ints into it. b is fully independent of a.

steps.name: Mutate the copy
steps.detail: `b[0] = 99` changes only b's block: b is [99 20 30] while a stays [10 20 30]. Value semantics keep them separate.

steps.name: Pass to a function
steps.detail: Calling `f(a)` copies the whole array onto the call. The callee can read or mutate its copy, but a in the caller is untouched — pass *[3]int or a slice to share.

interactiveExamples.title: Arrays copy; slices would share
interactiveExamples.explanation: b := a copies every element, so changing b[0] never touches a. This value-copy behavior is the single most important thing that separates arrays from slices.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := [3]int{10, 20, 30} // fixed-size array, type [3]int
	b := a                  // COPY: b is an independent array
	b[0] = 99               // mutate only b's copy
	fmt.Println("a =", a)   // unchanged
	fmt.Println("b =", b)   // first element changed
	fmt.Println("a == b?", a == b) // arrays of comparable elems use ==
}

interactiveExamples.title: Zero values, literals, and the ... ellipsis
interactiveExamples.explanation: An undeclared array is zero-filled. [...]int{...} lets the compiler count the elements while still producing a fixed-size array (note len, not a slice). for-range is the idiomatic way to iterate.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var zeros [3]int            // every element is the zero value: 0
	primes := [...]int{2, 3, 5, 7} // compiler counts -> type [4]int

	fmt.Println("zeros:", zeros)
	fmt.Println("len(primes):", len(primes))

	sum := 0
	for i, v := range primes {  // i is index, v is a COPY of the element
		sum += v
		_ = i
	}
	fmt.Println("sum:", sum)
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: make the function actually update the array
interactiveExamples.explanation: double() receives a COPY of the array, so the caller's data never changes. Edit the code so the change is visible to main — take a pointer to the array (*[4]int) instead of the array by value.

checkpoints.code:
a := [3]int{1, 2, 3}
b := a
b[0] = 100
fmt.Println(a, b)
checkpoints.explanation: b := a copies the whole array, so b is independent of a. Writing b[0] = 100 changes only b. a stays [1 2 3] while b becomes [100 2 3].

checkpoints.prompt: Why does this function fail to compile?
options: [3]int and [4]int are different types, so x can't be passed to sum
checkpoints.explanation: An array's length is part of its type. [3]int and [4]int are distinct, incompatible types, so a [3]int value cannot be passed where a [4]int is expected. Slices ([]int) avoid this rigidity.

checkpoints.prompt: This is supposed to print 5, but it panics. Why?
options: Index 3 is out of range for a 3-element array (valid indices are 0..2); a runtime index is not caught at compile time
checkpoints.explanation: Valid indices for [3]int are 0, 1, 2. Index 3 is out of range. Because i is a variable, the compiler can't catch it; the runtime panics with 'index out of range [3] with length 3'. A constant index a[3] would instead be a compile error.

checkpoints.prompt: Declare an array of 4 ints and let the compiler count the elements.
checkpoints.explanation: [...]int{2, 3, 5, 7} tells the compiler to count the literal's elements and set the length, producing a fixed-size [4]int. []int{...} and make([]int, 4) create slices, not arrays, and [4]int{} would be all zeros.

codeLab.title: Rotate a fixed-size array right by one
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(a [5]int) [5]int` that returns a NEW array with every element shifted one position to the right, wrapping the last element around to the front. The input must not be modified — lean into array value semantics.
hints: Declare a fresh `var out [5]int` so the input is never mutated.
Element at index i should land at index (i+1)%n so the last element wraps to the front.
Because arrays are values, simply `return out` hands back an independent copy — and `==` compares them element by element in the test.

debuggingLab.title: Mutations to a function's array argument vanish
debuggingLab.symptom: scaleAll is supposed to triple every element, but after the call the array is unchanged.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Arrays are value types. Passing `nums` to scaleAll copies all three elements into the parameter `a`. The loop mutates that local copy, not the caller's array, so main's `nums` is never touched. Unlike slices (which share a backing array), arrays do not let a callee see mutations through the parameter.
commonMistakes: Assuming arrays behave like slices and are shared with the callee.
Forgetting that every array assignment and argument pass is a full copy.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Pass a pointer to the array (*[3]int) so the function mutates the caller's data, or return the modified array and assign it back.

theory.question: How does an array differ from a slice in Go?
theory.directAnswer: An array has a fixed length that is part of its type ([3]int vs [4]int are different types) and is a value type, so assigning or passing it copies every element. A slice is a small header (pointer, length, capacity) that views a backing array, is dynamically sized, and is shared rather than copied — copying a slice copies only the header, not the data. In practice you almost always use slices.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An array is a fixed-size contiguous block; a slice is a growable, reference-like view over an underlying array.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Arrays give a precise, fixed memory layout; slices add the flexibility of variable length on top of arrays, which is what most code needs.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: An array's length is a compile-time constant baked into its type and copies on assignment; a slice header points into a backing array and is passed by value (the header), so both copies see the same data.

theory.whyImportant: The copy-vs-share distinction drives correctness: arrays prevent accidental aliasing but can't be resized, while slices are flexible but can alias. It's a near-guaranteed interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: sha256.Sum256 returns a fixed [32]byte array (a precise, copyable value), whereas an HTTP request body is read into a []byte slice because its length varies.

followUps.question: What happens when you pass a large array to a function?
followUps.answer: The entire array is copied onto the call, which can be expensive. Pass a pointer (*[N]T) or, more idiomatically, a slice to avoid the copy.

followUps.question: Is [3]int assignable to [4]int?
followUps.answer: No. They are distinct types because length is part of the type, so there is no implicit conversion between them.

theory.question: When can you compare two arrays with ==, and what does it compare?
theory.directAnswer: You can compare two arrays with == when they have the same type (same length and element type) and the element type is itself comparable. == returns true only if every corresponding element is equal — it's an element-by-element comparison, not a reference check.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Built-in equality for array values of a comparable element type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Arrays are values, so it's well-defined to compare them by their contents, which also makes comparable arrays usable as map keys.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler emits an element-wise comparison; if any element differs, the result is false. Slices, by contrast, are NOT comparable with == (except to nil).

theory.whyImportant: Knowing arrays are comparable (and slices are not) explains why arrays can be map keys and is a common point of confusion in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: Two [16]byte UUIDs can be compared directly with == to check identity, and a [2]int coordinate can serve as a map key.

followUps.question: Why can't slices be compared with ==?
followUps.answer: Slices reference mutable backing arrays of arbitrary length; element-wise == would be ambiguous and potentially O(n) surprise, so Go only allows comparing a slice to nil. Use slices.Equal or reflect.DeepEqual instead.

followUps.question: Can an array be a map key?
followUps.answer: Yes, as long as its element type is comparable — e.g. map[[2]int]string works.

theory.question: What is the difference between `[3]int{1,2,3}` and `[...]int{1,2,3}`, and does the ellipsis create a slice?
theory.directAnswer: Both create a fixed-size array with the same elements; the only difference is who determines the length. `[3]int{...}` states the length explicitly, while `[...]int{...}` tells the compiler to count the literal's elements and set the length for you. The `...` form does NOT create a slice — the result is still a genuine fixed-size array whose length is baked into its type. Use `[]int{...}` (no length) to get a slice instead.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two array-literal forms: explicit-length and compiler-counted-length.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The ellipsis form spares you from counting elements by hand and keeps the length in sync with the literal, while still producing an array.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler counts the initializer elements and substitutes that count as the array length; the resulting type is [N]T, comparable and value-copied like any array.

theory.whyImportant: Beginners often assume [...] produces a slice or that it's dynamic; clarifying it's still a fixed array is a common interview clarification.
theory.realWorldExample: `days := [...]string{"Mon", "Tue", "Wed"}` produces a [3]string without manually counting — add a day and the length updates automatically.

followUps.question: What type does `[...]int{1, 2, 3, 4}` have?
followUps.answer: [4]int — the compiler counts four elements and fixes the length at four.

followUps.question: How do I make a slice literal instead?
followUps.answer: Omit the length entirely: `[]int{1, 2, 3}` is a slice, whereas `[3]int{...}` and `[...]int{...}` are arrays.

theory.question: When is an out-of-range array access a compile error versus a runtime panic?
theory.directAnswer: If the index is a constant known at compile time and it falls outside the array's fixed length, the compiler rejects it as a compile error (e.g. a[3] on a [3]int). If the index is a variable whose value the compiler can't prove, the check happens at runtime: an out-of-range value panics with 'index out of range'. So constant indices are caught early; variable indices are checked by the runtime's bounds check.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two layers of array bounds checking: compile-time for constants, runtime for variables.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The compiler knows an array's length statically, so it can catch obviously invalid constant indices; variable indices need a runtime guard to stay memory-safe.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: For constant indices the compiler compares against the type's length; for variable indices Go inserts a bounds check that panics rather than reading out of bounds (unlike C's undefined behavior).

theory.whyImportant: Understanding when errors surface (build vs. runtime) helps diagnose panics and is a common Go safety talking point in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: Reading a[userIndex] where userIndex comes from input can panic at runtime, so you guard with `if userIndex < len(a)` before indexing.

followUps.question: Does Go's bounds checking hurt performance?
followUps.answer: There's a small cost, but the compiler eliminates many checks it can prove safe (bounds-check elimination), and the safety is usually worth it.

followUps.question: What's the panic message for a bad variable index?
followUps.answer: Something like 'panic: runtime error: index out of range [3] with length 3'.

scenario.question: A teammate stores image pixels in a large [1024][1024]int array and passes it to helper functions by value. CPU profiles show huge time spent in memmove and the program allocates more than expected. What's going on and how would you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: Passing the array by value copies all ~1 million ints (~8MB) on every call — that's the memmove cost, and large copies can spill to the heap. Fix it by passing a pointer to the array (*[1024][1024]int) or, more idiomatically, switching the data structure to a slice ([][]int or a flat []int with manual indexing), so functions share one backing store instead of duplicating it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Accidental whole-array copies caused by array value semantics on every function call.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Arrays are values; passing one always copies it, and the cost scales with size.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each call duplicates the entire block (memmove); large enough copies may also force heap allocation and add GC pressure.

scenario.whyImportant: Misunderstanding array copy semantics is a real performance footgun in numeric and image code.
scenario.realWorldExample: Image-processing pipelines pass *[]byte or a slice of pixels, never large value arrays, precisely to avoid per-call copies.

followUps.question: When is passing an array by value actually fine?
followUps.answer: When it's small and fixed (e.g. [16]byte UUID) — the copy is cheap and the value semantics give you safe, independent data.

followUps.question: How would you confirm copies are the cause?
followUps.answer: A CPU profile (pprof) showing time in runtime.memmove on the call paths, plus an alloc profile showing large allocations tied to those calls.

scenario.question: A developer takes a slice of an array with `s := arr[1:4]`, then mutates `s[0]` expecting the original array to stay unchanged. It changes anyway, causing a bug. Explain why and how to get an independent copy.
scenario.directAnswer: A slice is a view over a backing array, not a copy. `s := arr[1:4]` makes s share arr's underlying storage, so writing s[0] writes through to arr[1]. This is the opposite of `b := arr`, which copies the whole array. To get independent data, allocate a new slice and copy into it: `s := make([]int, 3); copy(s, arr[1:4])`, or copy the array by value first (`cpy := arr`) and slice that.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The sharing (aliasing) behavior of slices versus the value-copy behavior of arrays.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Slices are lightweight views for efficiency; copying a slice copies only the header, so mutations alias the shared backing array.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: arr[1:4] builds a slice header pointing into arr's memory; writes through the slice hit the same bytes. Arrays instead copy fully on assignment, so a copied array is independent.

scenario.whyImportant: Accidental aliasing through slices is a leading source of subtle mutation bugs, and the array-copies-but-slice-shares contrast is a near-guaranteed interview question.
scenario.realWorldExample: Slicing a request buffer and mutating it before the original is fully consumed corrupts the data; copying with make+copy avoids the shared-backing bug.

followUps.question: How do you cheaply get an independent copy of an array?
followUps.answer: Just assign it: `cpy := arr` copies every element because arrays are value types.

followUps.question: Does re-slicing ever break the alias?
followUps.answer: Not by itself; only allocating new storage (make+copy, or append that triggers reallocation) gives independent backing data.

systemDesign.question: You're designing a content-addressed store keyed by SHA-256 hashes. Would you key the map with a [32]byte array or a []byte slice, and why?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Use the fixed-size array [32]byte as the key, not a []byte slice. A SHA-256 digest is always exactly 32 bytes, so the array's fixed length fits the data precisely, and arrays of a comparable element type are themselves comparable — which means [32]byte can be a map key (map[[32]byte]Value) and compared with ==. Slices cannot be map keys and aren't comparable with == (except to nil), so keying by []byte is impossible without converting to a string or array.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A design choice between a fixed-size array and a slice for a hash-keyed lookup table.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Map keys must be comparable; arrays of comparable elements qualify while slices do not, and fixed-width data maps naturally onto a fixed-size array.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: sha256.Sum256 returns a [32]byte value that copies cheaply and compares element-wise, so it drops directly into a map[[32]byte]V key with correct equality semantics.

systemDesign.whyImportant: Content-addressed stores (Git, Docker layers, dedup systems) rely on hash keys, and this decision showcases why array comparability and fixed-size value semantics matter.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: sha256.Sum256(data) returns [32]byte, so a dedup cache uses map[[32]byte][]byte to map a content hash to its stored blob.

followUps.question: What if you only have a []byte digest, not an array?
followUps.answer: Convert it: copy into a [32]byte (or use string(b) as the key), since the slice itself can't be a comparable map key.

followUps.question: Is copying a [32]byte key expensive?
followUps.answer: No — 32 bytes is tiny, so value-copying it into and out of the map is cheap and gives safe, independent keys.

coding.question: Implement `func Counts(s string) [26]int` that returns the frequency of each lowercase ASCII letter a-z in s (ignore any other character).
coding.thoughtProcess: A fixed 26-slot array indexed by (letter - 'a') is a perfect lookup table here: the size is genuinely constant, and an array gives O(1) indexing with no allocation. Iterate the bytes of s, and for each character in 'a'..'z' increment the slot at index c-'a'. Returning the array hands back a clean copy.
coding.lineByLine: freq is a [26]int auto-initialized to all zeros, used as a lookup table indexed by letter offset. We walk the string byte by byte; for each lowercase letter we compute c-'a' (0 for 'a', 25 for 'z') and increment that slot, ignoring everything else. The function returns the array by value, so the caller gets a safe, independent copy.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) where n is the length of s.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — the result is a fixed 26-element array regardless of input size.

followUps.question: Why use an array here instead of a map[byte]int?
followUps.answer: The key space is fixed and tiny (26 letters), so a contiguous array is faster (no hashing), allocation-free, and the size is part of the type — exactly what arrays are good at.

followUps.question: How would you handle full Unicode?
followUps.answer: Range over the string to get runes (for i, r := range s) and aggregate into a map[rune]int, since the key space is no longer small or fixed.

coding.question: Implement `func AreAnagrams(a, b string) bool` for lowercase ASCII strings, using a fixed [26]int frequency array. Compare the two arrays with ==.
coding.thoughtProcess: Two strings are anagrams if they have identical letter frequencies. A fixed [26]int array indexed by letter offset is the natural, allocation-free counter. I build one array per string, then rely on arrays being comparable with == (element-by-element) to check equality in one expression — a nice payoff of array value semantics.
coding.lineByLine: fa and fb are [26]int arrays auto-initialized to zeros. We index each by (byte - 'a') to tally letter frequencies for a and b respectively. Because arrays whose element type is comparable support ==, `fa == fb` performs an element-by-element comparison and returns true only when every count matches — meaning the strings are anagrams. No maps or allocations are needed.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n + m) where n, m are the string lengths.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — two fixed 26-element arrays regardless of input size.

followUps.question: Why can we compare fa and fb with == but not two slices?
followUps.answer: Arrays of a comparable element type are themselves comparable (element-wise), so [26]int supports ==. Slices are not comparable with == (except to nil); you'd need slices.Equal.

followUps.question: How would you support Unicode or mixed case?
followUps.answer: Normalize case first and switch from a fixed array to a map[rune]int, since the key space is no longer the fixed 26 lowercase letters.

keyTakeaways: An array's length is part of its type — [3]int and [4]int are different, incompatible types, and the length is a compile-time constant.
Arrays are value types: assigning or passing one copies every element, so a function can't mutate the caller's array unless you pass *[N]T (contrast slices, which share a backing array).
Elements are zero-valued on declaration; use [N]T{...} literals or [...]T{...} to let the compiler count, index from 0, and compare comparable arrays with ==.
You rarely use arrays directly — slices are preferred — but arrays back every slice and are ideal for fixed-size data like [32]byte hashes and [16]byte UUIDs.
